newsitem.title: CANADA: More Canada auto workers strike GM.
newsitem.headline: More Canada auto workers strike GM.

text.p: Another 5,690 Canadian auto workers were on strike against General Motors Corp. on Monday after joining 15,000 other unionized workers on the picket lines Sunday as contract talks failed to progress over the weekend.
Union workers at GM Canada's St. Catharines, Ontario, plant about 30 miles (48 km) south of Toronto began picketing at 9:15 p.m. EDT (0115 GMT Monday), GM spokesman Greg Gibson said.

The Canadian Auto Workers union began an escalating strike against GM last Wednesday at the carmaker's Oshawa, Ontario complex, about 30 miles (48 km) east of Toronto, after failing to convince the company that it should accept the labor deal forged with Chrysler Corp. at the end of September.
The union is set to send the last 5,000 of its 26,000 GM workers on strike by Wednesday at midnight if the world's largest automaker does not yield to its demands over outsourcing.

"We are disappointed that tonight's deadline has passed without us reaching a resolution with the Canadian auto workers on a contract settlement," said Dean Munger, GM Canada's lead negotiator. "We are hopeful that on Monday we can focus with the CAW on identifying approaches which meet the needs of our employees, our customers and our business."

CAW President Buzz Hargrove told an auditorium of striking GM workers in Oshawa on Sunday that talks began to break down last Monday after Munger offered and then retracted a deal on outsourcing that had encouraged the union.
"Mr. Munger, you are going to do at least what you said on Monday. The only question is when you are going to reverse those decisions," Hargrove told the cheering auto workers.
Hargrove said the union is looking to reverse GM's decisions on shifting work to outside companies, a practice known as outsourcing, that would cut 5,500 jobs.
He said he felt the talks had been sunk by GM CEO Jack Smith.

"I believe Jack Smith, the chief executive officer of General Motors, took the bargaining away from the Canadian negotiators and said, 'We're not going to settle. We're going to put it on hold and we're going to test the resolve of the General Motors workers in Canada,'" Hargrove said.
Hargrove said Friday that if GM bargaining did not show any movement by Monday, the union could open talks with Ford Motor Co. and set a strike deadline there.
He said he plans to meet with Munger on Monday morning, but was not hopeful that talks could get back on track.
"We need about 48 hours of hard work and commitment and this can be done," he said after the rally. "I haven't seen any of that yet."
During a question and answer period, one member complained that his unemployed friends were getting calls from GM to cross the picket lines at the Oshawa plants.
Hargrove warned GM that if one replacement worker crossed the lines his union would punish the entire industry with a shutdown.
"I want to say as clear as I can ... if they hire scabs at these plants we'll shut the goddamn auto industry down tight, every plant in the country," Hargrove said.
Analysts said a strike by all GM union workers in Canada could cost the automaker $100 million to $150 million a week and eventually force plants to shut down in the United States.
